scenes.text: Last time, we saw that losing the outer electron gets easier as you go down Group one. Now let's see what that looks like. Lithium, sodium and potassium are all Group one metals, called the alkali metals. Each atom has one outer electron, and each metal makes the same products with water. But drop them in, and lithium just fizzes calmly, while potassium bursts into flame. So why do Group one metals react so differently with water?

First, safety. You won't handle these metals yourself. They react with the moisture on your skin, so they're stored under oil and never touched. In school, these reactions are shown only as a teacher demonstration, or on video. So here, we'll watch them as short video clips. Rubidium and caesium, further down the group, are never used in schools at all.

Here's lithium. It's the least dense metal of all, so it floats, sitting high on the water, and it fizzes steadily as a gas is given off. It slowly moves around and gets smaller. It doesn't melt. A few drops of indicator in the water slowly turn pink around it.

Now sodium. It floats too, but the reaction is faster. It melts into a shiny silver ball that races around the surface, fizzing hard. It melts because the reaction gives out heat, and sodium melts at only ninety-eight degrees. If it's held still, it can even catch fire, with a yellow-orange flame. The pink spreads much more quickly.

And potassium. It melts at only sixty-three degrees, so it melts at once, and the gas it gives off catches fire straight away, burning with a lilac flame. It crackles, and it may spit. This is the most vigorous of the three we can show in a school.

Here's the surprise. All three make the same two products. The gas is hydrogen. The water becomes a solution of the metal hydroxide, which is alkaline, and that's why the indicator turns pink. For sodium, sodium plus water gives sodium hydroxide plus hydrogen. Lithium and potassium do exactly the same, each giving a fizz of hydrogen and a pink solution. So the difference isn't what's made. It's how fast.

Why the different speeds? In each reaction, every metal atom loses its one outer electron, and becomes a positive ion. The water takes that electron, which is what makes the hydrogen and the hydroxide. Last time, we saw that going down the group, the outer electron is further from the nucleus, with the same core charge, so it's held less tightly. Potassium gives up its electron most readily, so its reaction runs fastest. A faster reaction also heats the metal faster, so sodium and potassium melt, and potassium's hydrogen catches fire.
Quick prediction. Rubidium comes next in Group one, below potassium. What would happen if it touched water? Think about where its outer electron sits. Have a think.

Even more violent. Rubidium's outer electron is even further out, and its first ionisation energy is lower again. Rubidium and caesium react explosively with water, which is why we only see them in video footage. Caesium, below rubidium, is more violent still. The trend holds all the way down.

When you compare these reactions, the conditions must match. A bigger piece has more surface touching the water, so it reacts faster. Warmer water speeds things up too. So a fair comparison uses the same size of piece, the same amount of water at the same temperature, and a freshly cut surface. Change those, and you change what you see, without changing the metal.

That last condition matters. Alkali metals react with oxygen and water vapour in the air, so a dull film, called tarnish, forms on the surface. That's another reason they're kept under oil. Cut sodium, and the fresh face is shiny silver, but it goes dull within minutes. A thick film separates the metal from the water at first, so the reaction can start more slowly. A slow start doesn't mean a less reactive metal.
So here's the chain to keep. The further out the outer electron, the easier it comes off, and the faster the metal reacts. Further out, easier off, faster fizz.

Your turn. In a teacher demonstration, equal-sized pieces of lithium and potassium are added to water. Potassium reacts much more vigorously. Explain this difference in terms of atomic structure. Pause here to answer.

Both atoms react by losing one outer electron. Potassium has two more occupied shells than lithium, so its outer electron is further from the nucleus, with the same core charge. It's held less tightly, so potassium loses it more readily, and reacts faster. Saying potassium has more electrons to give away is the slip. Each atom gives up just one.

Last one. Two equal pieces of sodium are added to water at the same temperature. Piece A was freshly cut. Piece B had been exposed to air, and its surface is dull. Predict which piece starts reacting faster, and explain. Pause here to answer.

Piece A. Piece B is coated with tarnish, a film formed by reacting with the air, which keeps water away from the metal at first. Piece A's fresh metal touches the water straight away. Saying they react at the same rate, because they're the same element, is the trap. Same metal, different surface.

One last clue. Potassium's flame was lilac, and sodium's was yellow-orange. Hydrogen burning on its own has a pale, almost invisible flame. So the colour must come from the metal. You'll see the same colours whenever these metals' compounds get into a Bunsen flame. Next time, we'll see what flame colours can show, and what they can't identify reliably.
Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.
